source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Hesse's three criteria
finding: Hesse (1966) gave three requirements for a good scientific analogical argument: material analogy (pre-theoretic observable similarities, not just formal), a causal condition (vertical relations in the source are causal), and no essential difference (essential source properties and causal relations are not in the negative analogy).
numbers: 3 criteria. Hesse 1966 pages 68, 87, 91.
quote: vertical relations in the model [source] are causal relations in some acceptable scientific sense
limits: SEP calls all three 'on the right track' but too restrictive: formal analogy drives maths and physics (Steiner), correlation without known cause can still persuade (Franklin's 12-point lightning list, 1749), and the rectangle-box analogy has many 'essential' differences yet is good. Hesse aims at modal plausibility, not degrees of probability.
agent_relevance: The causal-link and no-essential-difference checks can be coded as a guardrail, but only as soft flags: a hard reject would kill good formal and correlational analogies.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Bartha's articulation model
finding: Bartha (2010) classifies analogies by the vertical relations inside each domain, not by overall similarity. A good argument needs Prior Association (a clear link in the source between the known similarities P and the projected feature Q, which fixes the critical features) and Potential for Generalization (no critical disanalogy in the target).
numbers: 2 conditions. Worked example: rectangles (square has max area for fixed perimeter) to boxes (cube has max volume for fixed surface area); check each assumption used in the proof for an analogue in 3D.
quote: there must be no critical disanalogy between the domains
limits: Aims at prima facie plausibility (worth investigating), not probability. Needs the prior association to be made explicit, whose standard varies (causal law, proof, function).
agent_relevance: This is the most codeable form: step 1 write the source derivation, step 2 list its assumptions, step 3 test each for a target analogue. Maps onto G2/G3 (check against something real, not opinion).

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - commonsense guidelines G1-G8
finding: Textbook rules: more similarities strengthen, more differences weaken, more ignorance weakens, weaker conclusion is more plausible, causal analogies beat non-causal, structural beats superficial, relevance must be considered, multiple analogies help. SEP says they are vague and can pull apart.
numbers: 8 rules (G1-G8). Example conflict: Reid's life-on-other-planets argument is 'suggestive' to Stebbing (1933, weak conclusion, G4) but rejected by Mill (1843, vast ignorance, G3).
limits: Most rules assume probability, but many analogical arguments only aim at prima facie plausibility. G7 (relevance) is the crux and is not defined by counting.
agent_relevance: Do not score analogy strength by counting matches. Count-based scoring is the thing the field has shown fails.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - failure of simple inference rule
finding: A rule 'infer Q with support p, rising with n positive analogies, falling with negative ones' justifies too much. Achinstein's swan/line-segment case: same-colour is reflexive, symmetric, transitive, as is congruence, yet no support for clustered congruent lines.
numbers: Rule (5) needs only n>=1 positive analogy. Achinstein 1964 p.328.
quote: The positive analogy is antecedently known to be irrelevant to the hypothetical analogy.
limits: Shows that formal parallelism is cheap. Relevance must come from subject knowledge.
agent_relevance: A code check on 'number of shared attributes' or 'shared structure' is not a valid pass test (G3). Needs a relevance test tied to the claim.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Mill sampling and Harrod
finding: Mill: analogy is a competition between known agreements and known differences; agreement in 9 of 10 properties gives probability 0.9 for another shared property, if both things are well known. Harrod (1956) put this as binomial draws from an urn. Two fatal problems: the counting problem (what is one property?) and the bias problem (the list of known features is partisan, not random).
numbers: 9/10 -> 0.9. Mill rejected Reid's argument because unknown properties are vast.
quote: a competition between the known points of agreement and the known points of difference
limits: The ratio shared/total changes a lot with how properties are individuated.
agent_relevance: A model asked to 'list similarities and differences' produces an advocate's sample. Count ratios from such lists are biased.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Keynes and Hesse a priori justification
finding: Keynes (1921) used the Principle of Limitation of Independent Variety to show that with no negative analogy, the positive analogy raises probability. With any nontrivial negative analogy the probability stays unchanged (Hesse 1966). Hesse (1974) added a Clustering Postulate (a built-in bias to generalize). SEP: a purely syntactic postulate cannot separate good analogies from worthless ones.
numbers: No numbers; qualitative result: zero learning once any negative analogy exists in Keynes's measure.
limits: Carnapian measure permits no learning from experience.
agent_relevance: Pure formal-probability justification of analogy fails; keep analogy as a hypothesis generator with separate testing.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Bartha modal justification
finding: Bartha justifies his criteria through van Fraassen's symmetry principle ('problems which are essentially the same must receive essentially the same solution'), made modal: if problems might be essentially the same, they might have essentially the same solution. Meeting the articulation criteria shows the first 'might'; prima facie plausibility is the second.
numbers: Scope: only arguments aiming at prima facie plausibility, with non-trivial positive analogy and no known critical disanalogy.
quote: problems which are essentially the same must receive essentially the same solution
limits: Very weak conclusion: a candidate worth investigating, not evidence.
agent_relevance: Matches G3/G8: an analogy output is only a hypothesis; it earns belief only after a test the answer was not fitted to.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - determination rules (Davies and Russell)
finding: If background knowledge says Q = F(P1..Pm) and source and target agree on every Pi, then Q(T)=Q(S) follows deductively. Weitzenfeld (1984) argues analogies are deductive arguments with an enthymematic determination-rule premise. Not a full justification, since often we do not know all the relevant factors.
numbers: Example: used-car value fixed by year, make, mileage, condition, colour, accident history. Counter-example: morphine and meperidine, where relevant factors are unknown.
quote: Q is a function of P1, ..., Pm
limits: The rule is as hard to justify as the analogy itself.
agent_relevance: Best fully checkable form: when a determination rule is known, code can verify the match of all P values and then copy Q. Otherwise unusable.

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - critique of structure mapping
finding: Systematicity (Gentner) is neither necessary nor sufficient for plausibility. McKay (1993): Antarctica to present Mars is more systematic than Antarctica to ancient Mars, yet freezing is a counteracting cause, so ancient Mars is the stronger case. Schlimm (2008): in object-rich maths domains maximal systematicity is trivial.
numbers: Example: microbes in frozen Antarctic lakes; Mars 3.5 billion years ago was warmer.
quote: There is no short-cut via syntax.
limits: Also cites that surface matches matter in ethnographic analogy (Moche pot marks).
agent_relevance: A structure-match score from the model is not a plausibility check. Test the sign of causal relevance (positive vs counteracting).

source: Bartha (2013 rev.) Analogy and Analogical Reasoning, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy - Norton and Bayesian accounts
finding: Norton: no formal schema for analogy is adequate; each inference is warranted by a local 'fact of analogy'. Bayesian options: minimal (analogy sets priors), liberal (priors may shift by plausibility argument, with no rules; Hawthorne 2012), and analogue confirmation (Dardashti et al. 2017, 'dumb holes' as lab analogues of black holes; contested because the positive analogy is not independently known).
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Analogue confirmation gains evidence from new observations in the analogue, so it avoids the van Fraassen objection to belief change without evidence.
agent_relevance: Use the analogue as a source of new test data (run something), not as proof by resemblance.

source: Norton (2011 draft) Analogy (chapter, material theory of induction) - two-dimensional account
finding: Hesse and Bartha use a table with a source column and target column: positive analogy P, negative analogy A and ~B, and the target projection Q*. Support is a trade-off between positive and negative analogy, but Norton found no simple formula in Hesse for how to weigh them. Hesse's wording: strength depends first on extent of positive vs negative analogy, second on the causal relation between the new property and known ones.
numbers: Example from Hesse: argument to humans on Venus is stronger than on the Moon because Venus is more like Earth.
limits: Bartha (2010 pp.15, 35) is the source of the schema.
agent_relevance: Gives the data structure for a code check: P list, A/B list, Q, and a relation type linking P to Q.

source: Norton (2011 draft) Analogy (chapter, material theory of induction) - Bartha's articulation model in detail
finding: Bartha allows four vertical relation types: predictive, explanatory, functional, correlative (first two deductive or inductive; last two inductive only). Plausibility is judged in two stages: stage 1 prima facie (positive analogy relevant to prior association, no critically relevant factor in negative analogy); stage 2 qualitative on strength of prior association, extent of positive analogy, multiple analogies.
numbers: Predictive/probabilistic case (Bartha pp.120-21): five determinants: strength of prior association, extent of correspondence, multiple favourable analogs, only non-defeating completing analogs, only non-defeating counteracting causes. Multiple analogies need a partial order 'is superior than'.
limits: Norton's complaint: the model calls on inference schemas for each relation type, so it must solve all of induction too.
agent_relevance: Gives a short checklist for code: relation type, strength, defeaters (counteracting causes), and number of independent analogies.

source: Norton (2011 draft) Analogy (chapter, material theory of induction) - material theory and failures of analogy
finding: Norton argues the warrant is a local 'fact of analogy' (e.g. Galileo: moon shadows and earth shadows are formed by straight sunlight), not general similarity. Joyce (1936) already conceded that analogy works only if M and P are causally linked; Norton says even that is not enough: water causally relates to seas and canals, yet the moon has no seas and Mars no canals. Heat as conserved fluid failed after Joule (mid 19th century).
numbers: Cases: Galileo moon mountains (success); lunar 'seas', Martian canals, fish and whales, caloric heat (failures). Also Reynolds analogy and the liquid drop model of the nucleus, checked empirically, not by a trade-off rule (Blatt and Weisskopf 1979).
quote: Even the most successful analogies in the history of science break down at some point.
limits: A causal link in the source is necessary but not sufficient. Norton's approach cannot be coded as a general rule.
agent_relevance: Causal-link check will pass bad analogies. Pair it with an empirical probe of the target (G3), and treat the 'fact of analogy' as a claim to be tested.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour - overview
finding: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003, 175B) was tested zero-shot on four analogy domains against humans: digit matrices (Raven-like), letter strings, verbal analogies, story analogies. It matched or beat humans on most, and the authors called this emergent analogical ability.
numbers: Letter strings: 57 UCLA students, 100 problems per type. Digit matrices: 40 instances x 32 subtypes. Story analogies: N=54.
limits: Training-data leakage cannot be excluded (authors admit this in the review file, per Hodel and West).
agent_relevance: Baseline claim that analogy is strong in LLMs. Later work narrows it.

source: Webb, Holyoak and Lu (2023) Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models, Nature Human Behaviour - story analogies (causal structure)
finding: Using Gentner et al. stories, each source story has two targets with the same first-order relations, only one sharing the causal relations. Humans and GPT-3 picked the causally matched target above chance, but GPT-3 lost in the far (cross-domain) condition and humans clearly beat GPT-3.
numbers: Human N=54: t(53)=21.3 overall, far t(53)=16.7; GPT-3 overall binomial p=0.0005, near p=0.0039, far p=0.065 (not significant). GPT-3 vs humans OR=0.37, p=0.0003, CI [0.21, 0.63]. 15/54 humans chose the analogous story every trial. GPT-4 (initial check) better, near perfect in the near condition.
limits: Only 18 story sets; GPT-4 result only in supplement.
agent_relevance: Direct test of the causal-structure criterion in LLMs: far analogies are where causal-relation sensitivity is weakest. A code check on causal link should not rely on the model alone for far-domain cases.

source: Hodel and West (2023/2024) Response: Emergent analogical reasoning in large language models
finding: Counterfactual letter-string variants (bigger interval, synthetic alphabet) broke GPT-3 but not humans. Only 'remove redundant letter' and 'sort' stayed comparable, likely because they need no new alphabet generation.
numbers: Compare original vs modified: humans stayed at similar level on all modifications; GPT-3 declined significantly on most types (exact counts not recorded). Counterfactual comprehension check: GPT-3 kept at least 30% of original accuracy except predecessor on the synthetic alphabet.
quote: GPT-3 performs well only for simple analogy problems with the standard English alphabet
limits: Zero-shot status not guaranteed; tests made for humans may not measure LLMs.
agent_relevance: Cautions against taking an LLM's analogy success as general: test on altered surface forms (a mutated input, G3).

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2024) Using Counterfactual Tasks to Evaluate the Generality of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Failed replication of generality. Letter-string analogies in permuted or symbol alphabets: humans stay high, all GPT models drop. GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 are no better than GPT-3 overall.
numbers: 136 Prolific participants (2 excluded). Mean accuracy over all alphabets and types: humans 0.753 [0.734,0.773], GPT-3 0.488, GPT-3.5 0.350, GPT-4 0.452. Error types: alternate rule use humans 38.59%, GPT-4 22.00%, GPT-3 5.81%; incorrect rule use GPT-3 30.97%, GPT-4 32.67%, humans 14.67%.
quote: may be more due to the presence of similar kinds of sequence examples in the training data
limits: Chat tuning may have hurt. Letter strings are an idealised domain; temperature 0.
agent_relevance: Treat model analogy answers as unverified when the surface form is unusual; GPT models rarely propose the inventive alternative rules humans do.

source: Lewis and Mitchell (2025, TMLR) Evaluating the Robustness of Analogical Reasoning in Large Language Models
finding: Extended robustness tests: digit matrices with the blank moved from the usual corner lose accuracy for GPT models but not humans; replacing digits by symbols changes little for either. Story analogies show answer-order bias and paraphrase sensitivity in GPT models.
numbers: Webb et al. data re-read: GPT-4 on 18 far-analogy stories was 89% (16/18) when the correct story was A and 61% (11/18) when it was B. Another model column: 1.0 (18/18) vs 0.72 (13/18). Pooled over presentations in one row, 0.78 (292/373).
quote: these models often lack the zero-shot robustness of human analogy-making
limits: Zero-shot simple prompts only; no chain-of-thought or reasoning models tested.
agent_relevance: Position bias in judging which analogy is better: always randomize and swap order in code and take only order-stable verdicts (G4, G5).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners
finding: Analogical prompting: the model first writes relevant solved problems of its own, then solves the target. Beat 0-shot CoT and (often) few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench with GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and PaLM 2; the text states an average gain of 4%.
numbers: Average accuracy gain +4% over baselines. Small models: retrieved labelled exemplars beat self-generated ones (text-curie-001, text-davinci-001); advantage appears only at text-davinci-002/003 scale. Error analysis of 50 correct + 50 wrong GSM8K/MATH problems.
quote: self-generation can fail if the LLM lacks sufficient strength or has not learned relevant knowledge
limits: Extra output tokens; common failure is a generalization gap (new problem harder than the self-made exemplars). No check that the exemplar is relevant in Bartha's sense.
agent_relevance: Source-domain recall helps, but without a prior-association or critical-disanalogy check it is only a prompt trick. Candidate: verify exemplar's solution steps and test each assumption on the target (articulation steps), counted at equal tokens (G7).

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024, ICLR) Large Language Models as Analogical Reasoners - scale boundary
finding: Self-generated analogs need a strong model: with weaker models self-generation fails to give useful or valid exemplars, and retrieved labelled exemplars win.
numbers: Table 4 (GSM8K): curie-001 and davinci-001 favour few-shot CoT with labelled exemplars; davinci-002/003 favour the analogical method. Exact per-cell values were garbled in the PDF text and are not recorded here.
limits: Exact accuracies not extracted.
agent_relevance: Gate analogical recall by model strength; for a small model, use retrieved verified examples.

source: Opielka, Rosenbusch and Stevenson (2025) Analogical Reasoning Inside Large Language Models: Concept Vectors and the Limits of Abstraction
finding: In Llama-3.1 (8B, 70B), small sets of attention heads give invariant 'concept vectors' for verbal relations (antonym, category) but not for abstract relations like previous/next. A concept vector can hold the right relation while the output is wrong.
numbers: 600 ICL prompts; Llama-3.1 70B reaches 98% on previous/next items but 62% on abstract previous/next tasks. Zero-shot steering: function vectors 50% (8B) and 58% (70B) vs concept vectors 14% and 2%. Concept invariance grows from 1 to about 5 examples, then plateaus.
limits: Two open Llama models only; linear representation assumption.
agent_relevance: Internal 'knowing the relation' differs from applying it: argues for an external code check of the mapped relation instead of trusting the answer.

source: Lee et al. (2025/2026, AAAI) The Curious Case of Analogies: Investigating Analogical Reasoning in LLMs
finding: Probing proportional and story analogies shows relational information is encoded in mid-upper layers when the answer is right; failures show it missing, or present but not applied. Patching the first entity pair from a correct case into a failing case fixes up to 38.4% of failures.
numbers: Patching gains: Exp 1 +32.3% / +38.4% / +35.6%; Exp 2 +25.9% / +38.1% / +30.5%; overall +49.8% / +61.9% / +55.3% (three model columns as printed). Linear probes separate analogical from merely lexically similar stories in middle layers.
limits: Column labels for the three results were not recoverable from the text extraction.
agent_relevance: Two failure modes to separate in a check: relation not extracted vs relation not applied to the target.

source: AnaloBench (2024) Benchmarking the Identification of Abstract and Long-context Analogies
finding: Tasks: pick the analogous story among 4 (T1) and retrieve analogs from a bank (T2). Performance falls as stories lengthen; top models near random at retrieval. Human-written analogies are 1, 10 or 30 sentences.
numbers: T1 accuracy (random 25%): 1 sentence GPT-4 89.1%, Claude 68.2%, human 96.0%; 10 sentences GPT-4 66.5%, human 72.5%; 30 sentences GPT-4 60.7%, human 73.3%. Model-to-column mapping read from table order (17 values for 17 labels). Humans agreed unanimously on 47/50 one-sentence analogies.
limits: Authors flag that GPT-4 may be advantaged on stories it extended itself; they re-tested with Claude-generated stories.
agent_relevance: Long, messy sources are where analogy selection breaks; an agent searching for a source analog should expect near-chance retrieval and verify it.

source: Calvo Figueras and Agerri (2025, EMNLP Findings) Benchmarking Critical Questions Generation
finding: Walton's critical questions for argumentation schemes (argument from analogy is the first example, e.g. 'Are your skin and mine similar?') were used to build a benchmark; 11 LLMs asked for 3 critical questions each.
numbers: 220 interventions, average 3.1 schemes each, annotated Useful/Unhelpful/Invalid by journalists and fact-checkers; no model exceeds 57% Useful on average zero-shot; best open model gemma-2-27b-it 54.03; best automatic evaluator claude_reference kappa 0.57 with manual labels.
limits: Not specific to analogy; the benchmark mixes schemes. No analogy-only score reported.
agent_relevance: Critical questions work as a checklist for 'no essential difference', but models fill only about half with useful items; use them to trigger tests, not as the verdict.

source: Gap statement for this angle
finding: No study found that tests an LLM on judging analogical-argument strength by Hesse's or Bartha's criteria, nor an LLM implementation of the articulation model. Searches found only analogy-solving and critical-question benchmarks.
numbers: 0 direct studies found; searches limited (WebSearch budget exhausted, OpenAlex rate-limited, arXiv API returned empty).
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search, not proof. Lee and Holyoak (2008) causal models in analogical inference and the Bartha (2010) book itself were NOT opened.
agent_relevance: The articulation checklist for our agent would be untested territory; plan an own measurement.
